summary:
We developed a harmonization system that links NASA’s two generations of active-fire data, MODIS (Terra/Aqua, 2000 onward) and VIIRS (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21, 2012 onward), into one continuous, comparable fire record for South America. Because VIIRS has a finer resolution, it detects about 3.9 times more hotspots than MODIS. Without correction, the 25-year record shows a false jump in fire activity when the sensors change.

Our method calibrates a multiplier k on 2012–2018 and tests it on 2019–2024. A single k predicts annual totals within 1.6% of the actual VIIRS counts. Refining k by country, quarter and day/night lowers the country-month error to 9.8%, compared with 74% when no correction is applied. The results are exposed through an API and an interactive dashboard that shows the multipliers per country.

This matters because trend analysis, climate research and fire management all depend on long records that stay consistent as sensors are replaced. Our approach is transparent, measurable and reproducible, and it can be extended to other regions and to the newer NOAA-21 satellite.
details:
What it does. The project ingests NASA FIRMS active-fire detections from MODIS (Terra/Aqua), VIIRS S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 for 14 South American countries, about 80 million hotspot records from 2000 to 2025. It stores them in a PostGIS database and turns them into a single, comparable fire record. Because VIIRS detects about 3.9 times more hotspots than MODIS, we calibrate a multiplier k on 2012–2018 and validate it on 2019–2024. We compared six schemes: no correction, a single k, day/night, per country, country × day/night, and country × quarter × day/night (112 values).

How it works. A Spring Boot REST API serves a fire calendar, per-country detail views and the harmonized series. A React and Leaflet dashboard shows the maps, the time series and a panel with the k multipliers per country, quarter and day/night. A reproducible Python pipeline handles extraction, k estimation, validation and reporting.

Benefits and impact. Researchers, climate analysts and fire managers get a long, consistent record that does not jump when the sensor changes. The error is measured, not assumed. A single k predicts annual totals within 1.6%, and the best scheme brings the country-month error to 9.8%, compared with 74% without correction.

Tools. Java 21, Spring Boot, Flyway, PostgreSQL/PostGIS 16, Testcontainers, Python, TypeScript, React 19, Leaflet, Vite, Vitest and Docker Compose.

Creativity. We treat harmonization as a testable forecast: calibrate on one period, predict another, and report the error honestly.

Factors considered. Sensor resolution differences, day/night detection behavior, seasonality, small countries with little data
